ratings.reviewer_notes: LPS activates BV2 microglia and induces IL-18, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6, but these cytokines are measured as downstream products in an LPS neuroinflammation model rather than tested as mediators of microglial activation in an AD model.

AD-derived human microglia and Aβ-treated cultures produce IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and M-CSF; useful AD-specific context, but the cytokines are primarily reported as products of activated microglia rather than upstream activators.
AD-focused review links activated microglia with IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α production and discusses inflammatory signaling, but does not directly test these cytokines as causes of microglial activation.
In 5xFAD and Tg2576 mice, hearing loss increases microglial markers alongside IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. This is associative AD-model evidence, not a test of cytokine-mediated activation.
LPS-activated microglia release TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, with DHT suppressing this response. It is a non-AD LPS model and treats cytokines mainly as activation outputs.
Directly tests IFN-γ plus TNF-α as pro-inflammatory microglial stimuli and IL-4/IL-10 as resolving cytokines, but uses primary rat microglia without an AD model.
Broad review of inflammatory mediators across AD, Parkinson disease, and multiple sclerosis; it does not identify cytokines that specifically mediate microglial activation in AD models.

In an STZ-induced AD-like mouse model, exosomes reduce microglial hyperactivation together with IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. The cytokines are correlated downstream inflammatory markers rather than tested activators.

Remimazolam reduces LPS-induced microglial activation and IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, but the study is a general LPS cognitive-impairment model rather than an AD model and does not test cytokines as upstream mediators.

In an Aβ oligomer AD model, activated microglia release a factor acting through TNF-α signaling to induce neuronal necroptosis. This directly supports TNF-α as a downstream effector of activated microglia, not as the trigger of activation.

Directly tests sustained IL-1β expression in APP/PS1 mice and shows microglial proliferation, extensive transcriptional reprogramming, and expansion of plaque-associated microglia that facilitates Aβ clearance.

AD-associated TOMM40 variants activate BV2 microglia and the NLRP3 inflammasome, causing release of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. These cytokines are downstream products rather than tested mediators of activation.

In LPS-treated mice and BV2 cells, galantamine lowers microglial markers and IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. This is an endotoxin model relevant to AD inflammation, but cytokines are measured as activation outputs.

AD neuroinflammation review discusses TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β and pathways controlling cytokine release from microglia, providing contextual evidence but not direct tests of cytokines as microglial activators.
P. gingivalis LPS induces IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in human microglial cells in a proposed AD-related mechanism. The cytokines are downstream inflammatory products, and no AD animal model is used.

Directly demonstrates in APP/PS1 mice and BV2 cells that IL-17A promotes microglial activation through TLR4/NF-κB and stimulates microglial TNF-α secretion; IL-17A neutralization improves pathology and cognition.

AD-focused review identifies IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α as cytokines elicited by Aβ-activated microglia. It focuses on cytokines released after activation rather than direct cytokine induction of activation.
Tests TREM2-bearing M2 microglial exosomes as a treatment for neuronal ferroptosis and inflammation; IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α are inflammatory readouts, not mediators tested for microglial activation.
AD review describes microglial activation states and production of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 after Aβ stimulation. It provides useful context but no direct cytokine-to-microglial-activation experiment.

In LPS-treated BV2 cells, the intervention shifts microglial phenotype and changes IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10, IL-4, and TGF-β. This is an in vitro LPS model, with cytokines used mainly as phenotype readouts.

AD review links NF-κB, MAPK, and TLR4 signaling to microglial release of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6. It supplies review-level context but treats these cytokines mainly as consequences and amplifiers of inflammation.
The GFAP-IL6 transgenic mouse directly links chronic IL-6 expression to early microglial activation and elevated TNF-α, but it is a general cerebellar neuroinflammation model rather than an AD model.

Different Aβ conformations activate rat microglia and selectively induce IL-1α, IL-1β, or IFN-γ release, while IL-6 and TNF-α are unchanged. Strong AD-related model evidence, but cytokines are activation outputs rather than upstream mediators.

AD neuroinflammation review covers interleukins, TNF-α, chemokines, inflammasomes, and microglia, offering relevant overview-level context without directly testing which cytokines cause microglial activation.
